treatment plan = an agreed set of steps for how a patient will be treated
follow-up appointment = a later visit to check how treatment is working
medical history = a record of past illnesses, operations, allergies and medicines
anaesthetic = a drug that stops you feeling pain during a procedure
MRI scan = a detailed image of the inside of the body made with magnets, not X-rays
operating theatre = the hospital room where surgeons perform operations
biopsy = removal of a small piece of tissue so it can be tested
GP = a general doctor you visit first, not a hospital specialist
the NHS = the United Kingdom’s publicly funded health service
A&E = the hospital department for sudden serious illness or injury
waiting list = a list of patients who must wait for a test, operation or specialist
health insurance = a policy that pays some or all of your medical costs
GP surgery = the clinic where a general practitioner sees patients
referral = a written request from a GP for you to see a specialist
consultant = a senior hospital specialist who leads a patient’s hospital care
outpatient = a patient who visits hospital for treatment but does not stay overnight
inpatient = a patient who stays in hospital overnight or longer
discharge = official permission to leave hospital after treatment
medical records = the written or digital file of a patient’s history and treatment
second opinion = advice from another doctor about a diagnosis or treatment
